Line of sight is important if we are talking about geographic features 1,000 feet high getting in the way (not that rare). That shields from the shock wave generated closer to the bomb, the light radiation, the wind that comes right after the shockwave to some degree, and from light radiation feeding the shockwave further at ground level (the blast of a nuclear bomb is from light radiation attenuating in air). Attenuation that occurs above a valley and the associated heat, is less able to cause airflow into that valley (nuclear wind), because the valley is a dead end flow wise, vs flat ground. That build up over space away from the blast site creates the massive flow that we see with nuclear bombs. That won't build as effectively over a mountain. So big single bombs can suck if there is terrain.
